title: How to Preach the Texts You Would Rather Skip
subtitle: A pastoral guide to preaching difficult Bible passages on judgment, hell, sexuality, and Old Testament violence without softening the text or losing the room.

sections.title: The Texts You Quietly Avoid
sections.body:
Every preacher keeps a list. He has never written it down. But he knows what is on it.

The passage on hell. The verses on sexuality the culture now treats as cruelty. The day God commands a city destroyed and the women and children with it. The wives submit, the slaves obey, the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart. We do not announce that we skip these. We arrange not to arrive at them. We choose a different series. We jump the awkward paragraph and call it focus. We preach around the wound and tell ourselves we are being wise.

I have done this. I have stood at the edge of a hard text and felt the cowardice dressed as discernment. The congregation never knew. That is the problem. They learned, without a word from me, that the Bible has a section we do not read in this room. We did not delete the verses. We did something quieter and worse. We taught our people they were optional.

sections.title: Why the Hard Texts Are Not Optional
sections.body:
A gospel edited for comfort is no longer the gospel. It is a product.

Paul told the Ephesian elders he was innocent of their blood because he did not shrink from declaring the whole counsel of God. The whole. Not the parts that preach well in a culture that flatters itself. The doctrine of hell is not a medieval cruelty bolted onto a kind message. It is the measure of what the cross cost. Remove it and the crucifixion becomes sentiment, a gesture without a danger behind it. The hard sexual ethic is not the church being behind the times. It is the church refusing to let the times write its theology.

When you skip these texts your people do not become free of them. They meet them alone, online, in the mouth of someone who hates the faith, with no pastor who ever helped them think. You were not protecting them. You were abandoning them to whoever got to the passage first.

sections.title: Earn the Right to Be Hard
sections.body:
A difficult text demands more preparation than an easy one, not less. Most of the offense we cause is the offense of laziness.

Before you preach the conquest of Canaan, you had better know the four hundred years of warning, the measure of the iniquity that was full, the difference between a one-time judgment on a named people and a permanent command. Before you preach hell, sit long enough with the texts that you can speak of it without relish and without flinching. Before you preach on sexuality, know the difference between what Scripture forbids and what your own discomfort assumes. Read the people who disagree with you and find the strongest form of their objection, not the easiest one to knock down.

The goal is not to make the text comfortable. You cannot and should not. The goal is to make sure that when your people are offended, they are offended by what God actually said and not by your carelessness in saying it.

sections.title: Weep Where You Warn
sections.body:
The same hard truth lands differently depending on the face that carries it.

There is a preacher who handles the doctrine of hell like a man enjoying it, glad to consign the room to the fire. There is another who can barely speak the words. The text is identical. One of them you believe. Jesus wept over the city he was about to indict. The prophets who pronounced the heaviest judgments were the ones who lay in the dirt and grieved for the people. You do not get the authority to be hard until you have shown the people you would spare them if you could.

This is not technique. You cannot fake it. The congregation can smell a man who is settling scores from the pulpit. Preach the hard text the way a doctor delivers a diagnosis he wishes were not true. Tell them the truth. Tell them it grieves you. Then do not take it back.

sections.title: Every Hard Text Has a Bottom
sections.body:
The hard texts are not a detour from grace. They are the floor that holds it up.

Preach hell, and then preach the One who walked into it so that your people would not have to. Preach the conquest, and then preach the day God turned that same fierce justice on his own Son instead of the guilty. Preach the demand of the law, and then preach the only man who kept it on our behalf. The judgment is real, which is exactly why the rescue is not cheap. You do not soften the hard text by hurrying to grace. You let it sit, full weight, until your people feel what they have been spared.

Do not preach a sermon that leaves them only frightened. Do not preach one that leaves them only comforted. Leave them where the text leaves them, looking at a holiness that could have destroyed them and a mercy that chose not to. Let that be the weight they carry out the door.
